brief: October payrolls rose 165,000; the prior two months were revised up 84,000. The three-month average rebounded from -45,000 (Oct 2025) to 137,000 (Oct 2026), and the diffusion index moved back above 60%, meaning growth broadened across private-sector industries. Unemployment fell a tenth of a point to 4.1%. Construction employment fell 3,000 as workers rotate from residential to nonresidential building; NISA attributes this to excess, mortgage-rate-idled housing-construction labor filling data-center construction demand. That shift is lifting construction wage inflation without moving total wage inflation off its disinflationary path. NISA reads this as confirming the labor market has stabilized since the Fed's 2025 insurance cuts, in a Goldilocks zone justifying neither cuts nor hikes, with no evidence yet that wage inflation is strong enough to sway FOMC votes. NISA argues this is moot: the Fed is set to hike in December on inflation, and NISA expects, with low conviction, oil prices to drop in time to head off a third hike in March. Only after that energy shock passes can the Fed judge further tightening from labor data, a question NISA pushes to 2027, contingent on whether the newly elected political class constrains the AI infrastructure investment driving labor demand this year.
